blocks.text: In a similar way Schmidius in his Notes on this passage: the limbs, which formerly, in lively youth, were nimble like the locust, a leaping animal, now, as if weighed down by some burden, can no longer move. And Herm. Witsius in the Exercitat. in Cap. XII. Eccles. (in his Miscellanea Sacra, vol. 2, Exercitation 6), §. 22, for whom the locust denotes the limbs which in their natural state are lighter and more agile than the rest and raise themselves of their own accord (e.g. the head), but in old age grow limp, sink down and need support. Io. Bern. Koehler also takes these words of the old man's back, bent [III, 337] like a locust, in the Observatt. critice. ad Ecclesiastae Caput ultimum, in the Repertorium Literaturae biblicae et Orientalis edited by Eichhorn, vol. 16, p. 222, following Glassius (Phil. S. book 5, p. 488) and Geierus.

"Those who have thought of Tithonus, the old man changed into a cicada, have by a manifest error confused the cicada, a very different animal, with the locust; to say nothing of the fact that Tithonus is imagined as shrunken by old age and leanness, whereas for Solomon the locust either grows, or grows fat and is weighed down." So J. D. Michaelis in the Laudatio funebris Gesneri, p. 182 of the book cited above.

Paulus, the theologian of Jena, holds that חגב is the stomach (in his commentary on Ecclesiastes entitled Neuer Versuch über die Koheleth, in the Repertorium Literat. bibl. et orient. edited by himself, vol. 1), no doubt comparing (for he gave no reason for the German version given loc. cit.) the Arabic حُجَّابٌ [ḥujjābun], plural حُجُبٌ [ḥujubun], which among other things means the dia- [III, 338] phragm, as Golius reports, p. 577. For he translates the whole clause thus, p. 250: So lange man nicht schwer am Magen trägt, und seine Lust zum Essen schwinden sieht; so that the words יסתבל החגב would literally mean: the diaphragm will be heavy.

Not very different from this view is what Jerome has in his Commentary on this passage: It should be known that where our manuscripts read locust, the Hebrew has chagab, a word which is ambiguous among them. For it can be rendered both ankle and locust. It indicates the swollen legs of old men, weighed down by the swellings of gout.
For Eichhorn, in his Commentary on this passage, the smoke rising from the pit is the swarm of locusts itself, which from a distance presents the appearance of a dense cloud, or of smoke.
